div.ab: LXXVII. Cyninges horswealh, se ðe him mæg geærndian, ðes wer(egild) is CC hund scll'.
LXXVII. Cyninges horswealh, se ðe him mæge geærendian, ðæs wergield bið CC scill.
Regis horsþealh (id est equi [stabularius] Waliscus), qui sibi nuntiare possit ad eum, eius weregildum est CC sol.
{LXXVII} Cyninges horswealh, se ðe him mæge geærendian: ðæs wergield bið CC sciƚƚ.
A Welsh horseman in the king’s service who can act as his courier: his wergild is 200 shillings.
The wergeld of a Welsh horseman who is in the king's service and can ride on his errands shall be 200 shillings.
The king’s Welsh horseman, who can carry his messages, his wergild is 200 shillings.
Des Königs Marschalk [Wälscher Stallmeister?], welcher ihm Botendienste leisten kann, dessen Wergeld ist 200 Schill.
The king’s horse-thegn [Welsh master of horse?], who can carry messages for him: his wergeld is 200 shillings.

note.label: associated (Whitelock)
note.quote: Whitelock (1955: 402) associates this with the laadrincmann of Æthelberht §13 [L7]; Oliver 2002: 87–88 questions this connection.

div.note: horswealh. The word wealh is ambiguous in Old English, meaning cither a “Welshman” or a “slave”. From the context, I assume the former meaning here, the king’s service raising the status of the Welshman so that he is entitled to the wergild of an English freeman. By itself, the law could mean that an unfree horse-servant in the king’s service was to be paid for as a freeman, which would then remind us of Ethelbert 7.
